lessons.title: Lesson 1: Setting a clear goal
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a wish into a clear goal with a what, a how much, and a by-when.
This lesson builds toward: Given a wish for your community or a skill you want to grow, you will write a clear goal with what, how much and by when, and choose a first step, that you can really do with the time and help you have.
Leaders start with a clear goal. "Help the kids on my block read more" is a wish. "Run a free book swap at the community center on the first Saturday of next month and give away 50 books" is a goal.
A clear goal says what you will do, how much or how many, and by when. It should be something you can really do with the time and help you have.
An AI assistant can help you sharpen a goal. Ask: "Here is my wish: ... Help me turn it into a clear goal with what, how much and by when. Ask me questions first."
Step by step:
- Write down a wish for your family, work or community.
- Add what you will do, how much, and by when.
- Ask the AI to ask you questions and help sharpen it.
- Check that it is something you can really do.
Words to know:
- Goal: something specific you plan to do by a certain time.
- Deadline: the date by which something must be done.
Try it now: Write one wish for your community. Ask an AI assistant to ask you questions and help you turn it into a clear goal with what, how much and by when.
You can now turn a wish into a clear, doable goal.

check.q: What turns a wish into a clear goal?
options: Adding what, how much and by when
check.why: A clear goal says what you will do, how much and by when.

check.q: Your goal is to give away 1,000 books next week, alone. What do you do?
options: Keep it; big goals are best
Make it something you can really do with your time and help
Ask the AI to do it for you
check.why: A good goal is something you can really do with the time and help you have.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Solving problems step by step
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use four simple steps to work through a real problem.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real problem at home, work or in a group, you will solve it with four steps: name it, list options, pick one and check how it went, weighing a good point and a risk for at least three options.
Every plan hits problems. Leaders stay calm and work through them in steps: name the problem, list a few options, pick one, then check how it went.
AI is a good thinking partner. Describe the problem without private details and ask: "Give me three options to solve this, with one good point and one risk for each." For example: "Only two people signed up to help with our clothing drive."
You choose. You know your people and your community better than any AI does. After you try an option, look back: did it work? What would you do differently?
Step by step:
- Name the problem in one sentence.
- Ask the AI for three options, each with a good point and a risk.
- Pick the option that fits your people and situation.
- Try it, then check how it went.
Words to know:
- Option: one possible choice.
- Risk: something that could go wrong.
Try it now: Pick a real problem from your home, job or group. Ask an AI assistant for three options with a good point and a risk for each. Choose one and write why.
You can now work through a problem in four steps with AI as a thinking partner.

check.q: What is the last step in solving a problem step by step?
check.why: After trying an option, you look back to see if it worked and what to change.

check.q: Only two people signed up for your clothing drive. What do you ask the AI?
options: "Give me three options, each with a good point and a risk."
check.why: Asking for options with a good point and a risk helps you choose wisely.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Speaking up with confidence
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan and practice a short talk that asks people to act.
This lesson builds toward: Given a goal you want people to help with, you will write and practice a one-minute talk with a clear call to action, practiced out loud and improved once with AI feedback.
Confidence grows with practice. A short talk is easier when it has a simple shape: why it matters, what you want to do, and what you are asking people to do.
Write a one-minute talk (about 120 to 150 words). Then practice it out loud. You can type it into an AI assistant and ask: "Is this clear and friendly? Give me two ways to make it stronger. Keep it under one minute."
Nerves are normal. Breathe slowly, look at a few friendly faces, and speak a little slower than you think you need to. Practicing in front of a mirror or one friend helps too.
Step by step:
- Write why it matters, what you want to do, and what you are asking.
- Keep it to about one minute.
- Ask an AI for two ways to make it stronger.
- Practice out loud three times, slowly.
Words to know:
- Call to action: the part of a talk that tells people exactly what you want them to do.
Try it now: Write a one-minute talk about the goal from Lesson 1. Ask an AI assistant for two ways to make it stronger, then practice it out loud three times.
You can now plan and practice a short talk with a clear call to action.

check.q: What is the simple shape of a short talk?
options: Why it matters, what you want to do, and your ask
A long story, a joke and a goodbye
check.why: This shape keeps a talk short and tells people what to do.

check.q: Your hands shake before your talk. What helps?
options: Breathe slowly and speak a little slower
Talk as fast as you can
check.why: Slow breathing and slower speech help calm nerves.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Giving and asking for feedback
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Give kind, useful feedback and ask for it.
This lesson builds toward: After working with a helper, coworker or family member, you will give kind, useful feedback and ask for feedback yourself, with one thing that went well, one thing to try next time, and thanks.
Feedback is information that helps someone do better. Good leaders give it kindly and ask for it often.
A simple way to give feedback: say one thing that went well, one thing to try next time, and thank them. For example: "You set up the tables fast. Next time, let's put the sign-in sheet by the door. Thank you for coming early."
Ask for feedback too: "What is one thing I could do better at our next meeting?" You can practice with an AI: describe a situation and ask it to help you word feedback that is kind and clear.
Step by step:
- Say one thing that went well.
- Say one thing to try next time.
- Thank the person.
- Ask others: "What is one thing I could do better?"
Words to know:
- Feedback: information that helps someone see what went well and what to improve.
Try it now: Think of a helper, coworker or family member. Ask an AI assistant to help you word kind feedback with one thing that went well and one thing to try next time. Say it out loud.
You can now give kind, useful feedback and ask for it.

check.q: Which is the last part of the feedback shape in this course?
check.why: Kind feedback ends by thanking the person.

check.q: You want to get better at running meetings. What do you ask your group?
options: "What is one thing I could do better at our next meeting?"
check.why: Good leaders ask for feedback often, with a clear question.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Leading a small project
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Break a project into tasks, give each a person and a date, and plan for problems.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small community project, you will break it into tasks with a person and a date for each and plan for two problems, with helpers picking tasks and a weekly check-in.
A project is a goal with a start and an end. To lead one, break it into small tasks, give each task a person and a date, and check in.
Ask the AI: "I am running a clothing drive at our church in four weeks. Break it into tasks with a suggested week for each. List two problems that might come up and how to handle them."
Share the task list with your helpers. Let people pick tasks they like. Check in each week, thank people often, and celebrate when you finish.
Step by step:
- Write your project goal.
- Ask the AI to break it into tasks with dates and to list possible problems.
- Give each task a person; let people choose.
- Check in each week and celebrate at the end.
Words to know:
- Project: a piece of work with a goal, a start and an end.
- Task: one small job that is part of a project.
Try it now: Use your goal from Lesson 1. Ask an AI assistant to break it into tasks with dates and list two problems that could come up, with a plan for each.
You can now plan a small project with tasks, people, dates and backup plans.

check.q: What should every task in a project have?
check.why: A person and a date make it clear who does what and by when.

check.q: A helper has not done their task by the date. What do you do first?
options: Check in kindly and ask what help they need
Do it yourself without telling them
check.why: Leaders check in and support helpers to keep them involved.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Planning your next skill
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose one future skill to learn and a first step to start it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a wish for your community or a skill you want to grow, you will write a clear goal with what, how much and by when, and choose a first step, that you can really do with the time and help you have.
The world of work keeps changing. Skills that help almost everyone include using digital tools, using AI well and safely, communicating clearly, working in teams, and solving problems.
Ask an AI: "Here is what I do now and what I enjoy. Suggest three skills that would help me grow, and one free way to start each." Then check the free options yourself, for example at your public library or an American Job Center.
Pick one skill and one first step you can do this week. Leaders keep learning, and they bring others along.
Step by step:
- Tell the AI what you do now and what you enjoy.
- Ask for three skills to grow and one free way to start each.
- Check the free options yourself.
- Pick one skill and one first step for this week.
Words to know:
- Future skill: a skill that will matter more as work and technology change.
Try it now: Final task: plan a small community project with one clear goal, two possible problems and how you would solve them, and a one-minute talk asking three people to help. Practice the talk with an AI assistant, get feedback, and improve it once.
You can now lead a small project with confidence and keep growing your skills.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear goal A wish without how much or by when. One goal with what, how much and by when that the learner can really do. Sharpened with the AI's questions and includes a first step. Problems and solutions Fewer than two problems, or no plan for them. Two possible problems, each with a chosen solution. Each solution shows a good point and a risk that were weighed. One-minute talk No talk, or no clear ask. About one minute with why it matters, what you will do, and a call to action asking three people to help. Practiced out loud and improved once using the AI's feedback. Project plan No tasks or dates. Tasks with a person and a date for each. Includes weekly check-ins and how helpers will be thanked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a future skill that helps almost everyone?
check.why: Clear communication helps in almost every job and community role.

check.q: The AI suggests a free online class for your next skill. What do you do?
options: Sign up and pay right away
Share your bank number to enroll
Check it yourself, for example with your library or job center
check.why: You check free options yourself before signing up.
